records.title: Free fall in a uniform gravitational field
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Free fall is motion under gravity alone. In a near-Earth uniform field, a body released from rest accelerates downward at g.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Imagine letting go of a ball where air has no effect. It falls faster each second because Earth pulls it downward.

records.title: Terminal velocity
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Terminal velocity occurs when drag balances weight, so vertical acceleration becomes zero while the body continues moving.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: A falling object can reach a steady speed when the air’s upward push balances its weight.
explanation: Terminal velocity occurs when drag balances weight, so vertical acceleration becomes zero while the body continues moving.

Skydivers change posture to change area and hence terminal speed; the model represents a fixed posture.

records.title: Buoyancy
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Buoyancy is the resultant upward pressure force exerted by a fluid on an immersed object.

records.title: Archimedes principle
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Archimedes’ principle states that buoyant force equals the weight of the fluid displaced by an immersed body.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: Imagine replacing the underwater part of an object with water. That water’s weight tells you the upward buoyant force.

A ship’s hull can contain air while its total mass is supported by the water displaced by the submerged hull.

records.title: Angle of contact
records.subject: Physics
records.shortDescription: Contact angle describes how a liquid surface meets a solid, measured through the liquid. It helps determine whether a narrow tube shows capillary rise or depression.
records.ageAppropriateExplanation: A liquid can curve upward or downward where it touches a wall. The angle at that meeting point matters.
explanation: Contact angle describes how a liquid surface meets a solid, measured through the liquid. It helps determine whether a narrow tube shows capillary rise or depression.
In an ideal cylindrical tube, h=2γcosθ/(ρgr). Angles below 90° give rise, above 90° give depression, and 90° gives no net capillary height in this model.
Clean water on glass commonly wets the wall; actual angles depend on surface chemistry and contamination.

definitions.Contact angle: Angle between solid surface and liquid-interface tangent, measured through the liquid.
definitions.Wetting: Tendency of a liquid to spread over or adhere to a solid.

records.formula: h = 2γ cosθ / (ρgr) · θ in degrees in the controls
realLifeExamples: Clean water on glass commonly wets the wall; actual angles depend on surface chemistry and contamination.
